text: Does 2 Thessalonians 3:10 indicate that
there should be strict work requirements
associated with SNAP benefits?
Hey everybody, I'm Dan McClellan, I'm a
scholar of the Bible and religion. And
as the Trump administration stands
poised to allow SNAP benefits to go
away, there are a lot of Christian
nationalists appealing to 2
Thessalonians 3:10 to endorse their
opposition to a welfare state and the
notion that nobody should get any
welfare unless they are meeting work
requirements. And here is 2
Thessalonians 3:10 from the NRSVUE. It
says, "For even when we were with you,
we gave you this command: Anyone
unwilling to work should not eat." And
Christian nationalists are basically
generalizing this to all times and
places so that it can be leveraged to
endorse contemporary ideas about work
requirements associated with any kind of
welfare. And this is a rank and ignorant
tergiversation of what's going on in 2
Thessalonians 3. There are specific
situations that are giving rise to this
passage. And while there are a couple of
different ways to interpret what's going
on here and what exactly this is about,
none of them support the Christian
nationalist leveraging of this verse
over and against SNAP benefits for folks
who cannot work. Now, the most popular
interpretation is that this is a
reference to folks within early
Christian congregations who were taking
seriously the notion that the eschaton
was imminent, that the end of the world,
the second coming, was going to happen
at any moment. And so, they rested on
their laurels. They thought, "Why do I
need to work and continue to earn a
living if everything's coming to an end
any day now anyways?" And so, I think
the majority of scholars would probably
say this is directed against people who
are saying, "I'm going to enjoy the
benefits of participation in the
Christian community without actually
working for my own upkeep because the
end times are happening at any moment."
This is not really about the
marginalized or the poor and certainly
not the disabled. This is about people
who are fairly well-off, but are just
deciding to coast into the eschaton
rather than continue to work. Now,
there's another reading that I think
makes an awful lot of sense, but is a
minority view of scholars. And this
reading is that this is really about
folks who are already employed in
certain church duties and are suggesting
that's all the work they should need to
do to be supported by the church. They
shouldn't have to go out and get outside
jobs to maintain their food, their
clothing, their shelter. And this
passage is saying, "No, you do have to
go out and support yourself in addition
to fulfilling your obligations to the
church congregation." And here are a
bunch of commentaries you can check out
if you would like to see examples of
scholars endorsing certain readings of
this passage. None of these readings
support the generalizing of this verse
to contemporary debates about work
requirements associated with SNAP. That
is just Christian nationalists putting
dogma over data because they want to
leverage the authority of the Bible to
endorse their Christian nationalism. And
that is again a tergiversation of this
passage from the Bible. And the fit for
this video
has been Powerman, aka Luke Cage.
